original: Opened 2000 in former Bankside Power Station
final_text: Tate Modern was opened by the Queen on 11 May 2000 inside Bankside Power Station, Sir Giles Gilbert Scott's power station, which closed in 1981.

original: Herzog & de Meuron architecture - industrial cathedral
final_text: Herzog & de Meuron kept Scott's 99-metre chimney and added a two-storey glass 'light beam' on the roof; Michael Craig-Martin's Swiss Light glowed atop the chimney until it was dismantled in May 2008.
source_note: 99 m chimney, glass roof extension, Swiss Light

original: Turbine Hall: massive commissions (Ai Weiwei sunflower seeds, Olafur Eliasson sun)
final_text: Turbine Hall commissions: Eliasson's The Weather Project (2003), a mist-veiled sun of mono-frequency lamps under a mirrored ceiling; Ai Weiwei's Sunflower Seeds (2010), 100 million porcelain seeds painted in Jingdezhen.
source_note: Tate: 100 million hand-painted seeds, Jingdezhen workshops

original: Free admission (special exhibitions paid)
final_text: The first Turbine Hall commission, on opening day 12 May 2000, was Louise Bourgeois's I Do, I Undo, I Redo: three 9-metre steel towers visitors could climb, guarded by her giant spider Maman, later acquired by Tate.
source_note: First Unilever Series commission; Maman acquired by Tate

original: Collections: Picasso, Dalí, Warhol, Rothko, Bacon, Hockney
final_text: Rothko gave Tate nine of his Seagram murals with exact instructions for wall colour, light and hanging height; they arrived in London on 25 February 1970, the same day he was found dead in his New York studio.
source_note: Murals arrived at Tate the day Rothko died

original: Switch House extension (2016) - 10 floors of twisted brick
final_text: The 10-storey Switch House (2016, now the Blavatnik Building) is a twisting pyramid clad in a perforated lattice of 336,000 bricks that glows at night; beneath it, the power station's round oil Tanks became galleries for live art.

original: 6 million visitors/year - most visited modern art museum
final_text: Tate Modern drew 5.25 million visitors in its first year, double the 2.5 million the three older Tates drew combined; it peaked at 6.1 million in 2019 and recorded about 4.6 million in 2024.

original: Views of St Paul's Cathedral across Millennium Bridge
final_text: The Millennium Bridge linking Tate Modern to St Paul's opened on 10 June 2000 and closed within days because crowds made it sway; fitted with 37 viscous and 54 tuned mass dampers, it reopened 22 February 2002.

original: Level 2: permanent collection by theme not chronology
final_text: At its 2000 opening Tate Modern rejected chronology and hung the collection in four themes: History/Memory/Society, Nude/Action/Body, Landscape/Matter/Environment and Still Life/Object/Real Life.

original: Members Room on Level 6 - London skyline views
final_text: Residents of the glass-walled Neo Bankside flats sued Tate over its 10th-floor viewing terrace; in February 2023 the UK Supreme Court ruled 3-2 that visitors peering into their homes was a nuisance.

original: Original Tate, opened 1897, Millbank
final_text: Tate Britain stands on the site of Millbank Penitentiary, demolished in 1890; Henry Tate paid for the building, opened by the Prince of Wales on 21 July 1897 as the National Gallery of British Art.
source_note: Tate history: Millbank prison site, 1897 opening

original: British art from 1500 to today
final_text: On 7 January 1928 the Thames burst its wall opposite the Tate, flooding the lower galleries: 18 works were lost and Turner's drawings were soaked in mud; the director fell into a flooded manhole and had to be rescued.

original: Turner Collection - largest in world (300+ oils, 30,000 works on paper)
final_text: The Turner Bequest, left to the nation at his death in 1851, holds nearly 300 oil paintings and about 30,000 sketches and watercolours, including some 300 sketchbooks; most of it is in Tate Britain's Clore Gallery.

original: Pre-Raphaelites: Millais, Rossetti, Hunt
final_text: For Tate's Ophelia, Millais painted the Hogsmill river at Ewell outdoors, then posed Elizabeth Siddall in a bath warmed by lamps; they went out, she fell ill, and her father billed Millais £50.
source_note: Tate: Hogsmill river, bath, £50 doctor's bill

original: Turner Prize awarded here annually
final_text: The Turner Prize, founded in 1984, is shown at Tate Britain only every other year; in alternate years it travels to venues such as Baltic in Gateshead, Turner Contemporary in Margate and Towner Eastbourne.

original: Clore Gallery for Turner
final_text: James Stirling and Michael Wilford's Clore Gallery, built to house the Turner Bequest, opened on 1 April 1987; its pediment over the entrance abstractly echoes the Tate's Victorian portico.

original: National Gallery: Old Masters, Impressionists (Van Gogh Sunflowers)
final_text: On 10 March 1914 suffragette Mary Richardson smuggled a meat cleaver into the National Gallery and slashed Velázquez's Rokeby Venus seven times in protest at the treatment of Emmeline Pankhurst.

original: Courtauld Gallery: Manet's "A Bar at the Folies-Bergère"
final_text: The Courtauld holds Manet's A Bar at the Folies-Bergère (1882), his last major work, painted in his studio with a real barmaid, Suzon, posing; the mirror reflection is impossibly shifted to the right.

original: Royal Academy: summer exhibition since 1769
final_text: The Royal Academy Summer Exhibition has run every year since 1769, through both World Wars, making it the world's oldest open-submission exhibition: anyone may send in work.

original: Serpentine Galleries: contemporary, free
final_text: The Serpentine opened in 1970 in a 1933-34 tea pavilion in Kensington Gardens; Zaha Hadid's 2000 anniversary tent, meant to stand one night, began the annual Serpentine Pavilion series.

original: Saatchi Gallery: controversial, YBAs
final_text: Charles Saatchi opened his gallery in 1985 in a disused paint factory on Boundary Road, St John's Wood; it moved to County Hall in 2003 and in 2008 to the Duke of York's Headquarters, a former military building in Chelsea.

original: White Cube: Damien Hirst's gallery
final_text: White Cube is Jay Jopling's gallery, not Hirst's: it opened in May 1993 in one small square room on Duke Street, St James's, and in its first decade never showed the same artist twice. Hirst was among its artists.
source_note: Founded by Jopling 1993, Duke Street room

original: Hauser & Wirth: mega-gallery
final_text: Hauser & Wirth, founded in Zurich in 1992, opened its first London gallery in 2003 inside a former bank on Piccadilly designed by Sir Edwin Lutyens; in 2014 it turned a Somerset farm into a gallery.

original: Founded 1929, 11 West 53rd Street
final_text: MoMA, conceived by Abby Aldrich Rockefeller, Lillie P. Bliss and Mary Quinn Sullivan, opened on 7 November 1929 in six rooms on the 12th floor of the Heckscher Building, 730 Fifth Avenue; it reached 53rd Street in 1932.

original: "Starry Night" (Van Gogh) - most famous work
final_text: MoMA acquired Van Gogh's The Starry Night in 1941 through the Lillie P. Bliss Bequest, whose terms let the museum sell works from her collection to buy new masterpieces.
source_note: MoMA: Bliss Bequest sales funded Starry Night

original: "Les Demoiselles d'Avignon" (Picasso)
final_text: MoMA bought Les Demoiselles d'Avignon (1907) in 1939, once owned by couturier Jacques Doucet, paying partly by trading away Degas's Jockeys on Horseback before Distant Hills from the Bliss Bequest.
source_note: Acquired 1939 via Bliss Bequest, Degas exchange

original: Monet's "Water Lilies" - immersive room
final_text: MoMA's first Monet Water Lilies, an 18.5-foot canvas bought in 1955, was destroyed on 15 April 1958 when a workman's cigarette set sawdust alight; an electrician died and 500 people were evacuated.

original: Warhol's "Campbell's Soup Cans," "Marilyn"
final_text: Warhol's Campbell's Soup Cans (1962) at MoMA is 32 hand-painted canvases, each 20 x 16 inches with a hand-stamped fleur-de-lis rim, first shown at the Ferus Gallery, Los Angeles, in his first painting show.

original: Sculpture Garden - Rodin, Picasso
final_text: Philip Johnson's Abby Aldrich Rockefeller Sculpture Garden (completed April 1953) set marble-paved terraces around shallow pools; Picasso's She-Goat and Rodin's Monument to Balzac have stood there.

original: Film archive - 30,000 films
final_text: MoMA's Film Library, founded in 1935 with Iris Barry as first curator, now holds more than 30,000 films and 1.5 million film stills.

original: Opened 1977, Beaubourg
final_text: The Centre Pompidou, open since 1977, closed on 22 September 2025 for a five-year overhaul (asbestos removal, new rooftop terrace) and is due to reopen in 2030.

original: Rogers and Piano architecture - inside-out building
final_text: Piano, Rogers and Franchini beat 681 entries in 1971 by putting the Pompidou's guts outside, colour-coded: blue for air, green for water, yellow for electricity, red for movement and safety.
source_note: Centre Pompidou: 681 entries; pipe colour code

original: Largest modern art collection in Europe
final_text: The Pompidou's Musée national d'art moderne holds over 100,000 works by some 6,400 artists, Europe's largest modern and contemporary collection and second in the world only to MoMA.
source_note: Largest in Europe, second after MoMA

original: Matisse, Kandinsky, Duchamp, Magritte
final_text: Brancusi left his whole Paris studio to the French state on condition it be rebuilt exactly as at his death (1957); Renzo Piano rebuilt it on the Pompidou piazza in 1997, with 137 sculptures and his tools.

original: Views from escalator tubes
final_text: The Pompidou's glass escalator tube is nicknamed 'la Chenille' (the Caterpillar); Jean Widmer put it at the heart of the 1977 logo, and some 250 million people had ridden it by 2020.
source_note: Pompidou: la Chenille, logo, 250 million riders

original: Pompidou-Metz: branch in Lorraine (2010)
final_text: Centre Pompidou-Metz, by Shigeru Ban, opened on 12 May 2010 under a woven timber roof said to be inspired by a Chinese hat; its spire is 77 metres high, a nod to the Paris centre's 1977 opening.

original: Former railway station (Gare d'Orsay)
final_text: Victor Laloux's Gare d'Orsay opened on 28 May 1900 for the Exposition Universelle as the world's first electrified urban terminus, its stone facade hiding a metal frame; it reopened as a museum in December 1986.

original: Impressionists and Post-Impressionists
final_text: Courbet's L'Origine du monde (1866), commissioned by diplomat Khalil-Bey and kept behind a curtain, later belonged to psychoanalyst Jacques Lacan; it entered the Musée d'Orsay in 1995 in lieu of inheritance tax.
source_note: Orsay: Lacan provenance, entered 1995 by dation

original: Monet, Renoir, Degas, Van Gogh, Gauguin, Cézanne
final_text: Painter Gustave Caillebotte left his Impressionist collection to France in 1894; after two years of wrangling the state accepted only about 40 works, now the core of Orsay's Impressionists.
source_note: Caillebotte bequest partly accepted after negotiation

original: The clock - giant windows overlooking Seine
final_text: On Orsay's fifth floor, at the exit of the Impressionist gallery, Café Campana sits behind one of the giant station clocks; through its glass face you see across the Seine to the Louvre and Sacré-Cœur.
source_note: Café Campana behind clock, fifth floor

original: Rooftop restaurant with Sacré-Cœur view
final_text: Orsay has no rooftop restaurant: its Restaurant, a listed historic monument, is the 1900 dining room of the station hotel, with ceilings painted by Gabriel Ferrier and Benjamin-Constant.
source_note: Former hotel dining room, Ferrier ceilings

original: New York (1959): Frank Lloyd Wright spiral
final_text: Frank Lloyd Wright worked on the Guggenheim's spiral for about 15 years but died in April 1959, six months before it opened on Fifth Avenue on 21 October 1959.

original: Bilbao (1997): Frank Gehry titanium curves - changed city
final_text: Gehry's titanium Guggenheim Bilbao opened on 18 October 1997; its 130-metre-long Arcelor gallery holds Richard Serra's The Matter of Time, eight walk-through sculptures of 5-cm weathering steel.
source_note: Opened Oct 1997; Serra in 130 m gallery

original: Venice: Peggy Guggenheim Collection, Grand Canal
final_text: Peggy Guggenheim's ashes lie in the garden of her unfinished Grand Canal palazzo, Palazzo Venier dei Leoni, beside the graves of her 14 dogs under the inscription 'Here lie my beloved babies'.
source_note: Buried in garden beside her dogs

original: Abu Dhabi: under construction, Jean Nouvel
final_text: Guggenheim Abu Dhabi is by Frank Gehry, not Jean Nouvel (who built Louvre Abu Dhabi); first announced in 2006, the Saadiyat Island museum, the network's largest, was set to open on 11 December 2026.

original: Broad (Los Angeles): Koons, Basquiat, Hirst, free admission
final_text: The Broad opened on 20 September 2015 with free general admission; Diller Scofidio + Renfro designed the 120,000-sq-ft building around a 'veil-and-vault' concept.

original: LACMA (Los Angeles): Urban Light installation, 202 streetlamps
final_text: Chris Burden's Urban Light (2008) at LACMA is 202 restored 1920s-30s cast-iron Los Angeles street lamps of 17 designs; he bought the first at the Rose Bowl flea market and painted them all one grey.
source_note: 202 lamps, flea market origin, uniform grey

original: SFMOMA (San Francisco): Snøhetta expansion, Richter, Warhol
final_text: SFMOMA reopened on 14 May 2016 with Snøhetta's expansion behind Mario Botta's 1995 building, partly to show the Doris and Donald Fisher Collection, lent for 100 years.

original: Art Institute of Chicago: "American Gothic," Impressionist collection
final_text: A judge called Grant Wood's American Gothic a 'comic valentine', but at the Art Institute's 1930 annual it won a bronze medal and a $300 prize and entered the collection.

original: Reina Sofía (Madrid): Picasso's "Guernica"
final_text: Guernica reached Madrid from MoMA on 10 September 1981 and hung in the Prado's Casón del Buen Retiro until July 1992, when it moved to its purpose-built room at the Reina Sofía.
source_note: Reina Sofía: Casón 1981-1992, then Reina Sofía

original: Stedelijk (Amsterdam): modern design, Van Gogh nearby
final_text: The Stedelijk's 2012 extension by Benthem Crouwel is nicknamed 'the Bathtub': a seamless white fibre-reinforced shell on just six supports that moved the entrance to Museumplein.

original: Louisiana (Denmark): sculpture park, Øresund views
final_text: Louisiana, the Øresund-side museum Knud W. Jensen opened in 1958, kept the name of the 1855 villa: its builder, Alexander Brun, married three women all named Louise.
source_note: Named for Brun's three wives named Louise

original: Museum Ludwig (Cologne): Pop Art, German Expressionism
final_text: Museum Ludwig was founded in 1976 when Peter and Irene Ludwig gave Cologne 350 works; it holds Europe's largest Pop Art collection and the world's third-largest Picasso collection.
source_note: Museum Ludwig: 1976 gift; Pop Art, Picasso

original: Art Basel: Basel, Miami Beach, Hong Kong - the art Olympics
final_text: Art Basel was started in 1970 by Basel gallerists Ernst Beyeler, Trudl Bruckner and Balz Hilt; it added Miami Beach (2002), Hong Kong (2013), Paris (2022) and Qatar (2026).

original: Frieze: London, New York, Los Angeles - contemporary focus
final_text: Frieze, founded in 2003 by frieze magazine's Amanda Sharp and Matthew Slotover, opened in Regent's Park and grew from 27,700 visitors to 105,000 by 2016; New York came in 2012, LA in 2019, Seoul in 2022.

original: FIAC: Paris, Grand Palais
final_text: FIAC, first held in 1974 at the Gare de la Bastille, ended after 2021 when the Grand Palais gave its October slot to Art Basel, which launched Paris+ par Art Basel in 2022.

original: Venice Biennale: every 2 years, national pavilions
final_text: The Venice Biennale opened on 30 April 1895 in the presence of the Italian King and Queen; Belgium built the first national pavilion in 1907, followed by Germany, Britain and Hungary in 1909.

original: documenta: Kassel, Germany, every 5 years
final_text: Arnold Bode founded documenta in 1955 as a side event of Kassel's federal garden show, to reconnect Germany with art the Nazis banned; held every five years, each lasts 100 days.

original: Armory Show: New York, since 1994
final_text: The Armory Show began in 1994 as the Gramercy International Art Fair in the Gramercy Park Hotel, run by five dealers; it took its name in 1999 on moving to the 69th Regiment Armory, home of the 1913 show.

original: YBAs (Young British Artists): Hirst, Emin, Ofili - Saatchi backed
final_text: The YBAs coalesced around Freeze, a July 1988 show Goldsmiths student Damien Hirst organised in an empty Port of London Authority building in Docklands, with Sarah Lucas, Gary Hume and others.

original: Neo-Expressionism: Basquiat, Schnabel, 1980s energy
final_text: Julian Schnabel's first solo show at Mary Boone in 1979 sold out before it opened; his large paintings on broken ceramic plates became emblems of 1980s Neo-Expressionism.
source_note: Mary Boone 1979 sold out; plate paintings

original: Street Art: Banksy, Kaws, Shepard Fairey
final_text: On 5 October 2018 Banksy's Girl with Balloon shredded itself in its frame at Sotheby's London after selling for £1,042,000; renamed Love Is in the Bin, it resold in 2021 for £18,582,000.

original: Digital/NFT Art: Beeple, Pak, generative art
final_text: Beeple's NFT Everydays: The First 5000 Days, a collage of daily images he began on 1 May 2007, sold at Christie's in March 2021 for $69.3 million, paid in Ether.

original: Installation Art: Kusama infinity rooms, Turrell light spaces
final_text: Kusama's Infinity Mirrored Room - The Souls of Millions of Light Years Away, a mirrored chamber of hanging LED lights about 4 metres square, is one of the most popular works at The Broad in Los Angeles.

original: Performance Art: Marina Abramović, Tino Sehgal
final_text: In The Artist Is Present (MoMA, 14 March-31 May 2010) Abramović sat silently for 736 hours 30 minutes as 1,545 people sat opposite her; Ulay appeared on opening night.
